title: Capgemini Exceller — Round 2 Technical Module Mock Test

questions.context: A team describes their new system as 'pre-trained on broad web text and then adapted to many downstream tasks like summarization and classification.'
questions.question: What best describes this system?

options.text: A relational database
A traditional if-else decision tree coded by hand
A foundation model
A rule-based expert system

questions.explanation: Foundation models are large models pre-trained on broad data, then adapted (fine-tuned or prompted) for many different downstream tasks.

questions.context: An LLM is asked to write a product description and produces fluent, grammatically correct text that includes an incorrect price.
questions.question: What does this best illustrate?

options.text: A syntax error in the model's code
Proof the model cannot generate any text
A hardware malfunction in the GPU
Hallucination — the model generated plausible but factually incorrect content

questions.explanation: Hallucination refers to confident, fluent output that is factually wrong — a known limitation of generative models.

questions.context: A company wants to generate marketing copy, product images, and code from natural-language prompts using one class of AI system.
questions.question: This class of AI system is best described as:

options.text: A hardware load balancer
Generative AI
Traditional relational database software
A static spreadsheet formula

questions.explanation: Generative AI systems create new content — text, images, code — based on learned patterns, rather than only retrieving stored data.

questions.context: A researcher explains that a model was trained once on a large dataset and now performs new tasks by seeing only 2-3 examples in the prompt, with no further training.
questions.question: This capability is best known as:

options.text: Database indexing
Few-shot learning
Supervised regression
Manual rule programming

questions.explanation: Few-shot learning is the ability of a pretrained model to adapt to a new task using only a handful of examples provided in the prompt.

questions.context: A chatbot answers a question about a well-known historical event with a confident, detailed, but factually incorrect account.
questions.question: What does this demonstrate about generative AI?

options.text: This proves the model has no training data at all
Fluency in output is not the same as factual accuracy
The chatbot is deliberately lying to the user
This can only happen with very small models

questions.explanation: Generative models optimize for plausible, fluent continuations of text, which is separate from factual correctness — hence outputs must be validated.

questions.context: A company chooses an LLM specifically because it can be adapted to legal document review, customer support, and code generation without being retrained from scratch for each.
questions.question: This flexibility is a defining trait of:

options.text: Single-purpose embedded firmware
A fixed lookup table
A manually coded decision tree
Foundation models

questions.explanation: Foundation models are valued precisely because one broadly pre-trained model can be adapted to many different tasks.

questions.context: An engineer notes that the model's knowledge reflects only information available up to its training cutoff date.
questions.question: What is the most direct implication of this?

options.text: The model may be unaware of events or facts that occurred after training ended
The model will refuse to answer any questions
The model retrains itself automatically every day
The model's answers about older topics are always wrong

questions.explanation: A static training cutoff means the model has no built-in knowledge of anything after that date unless given that information at query time.

questions.context: A generative image model is asked to create a photo of a bicycle with an unusual number of wheels and produces one anyway.
questions.question: What does this illustrate about how generative models work?

options.text: Generative models always verify physical plausibility before output
This means the model has a hardware defect
This is impossible and could never happen
They generate outputs based on learned patterns, which can combine into physically implausible results

questions.explanation: Because generative models learn statistical patterns rather than explicit physical rules, they can occasionally produce implausible combinations.

questions.context: A team debates whether their chatbot is 'intelligent' because it responds fluently to nearly any question.
questions.question: What is the most accurate characterization?

options.text: It is provably conscious
It cannot process language at all
It predicts likely next words based on patterns in training data, which can resemble understanding without guaranteeing it
It has the same reasoning ability as a human in every case

questions.explanation: LLMs generate text by predicting likely continuations based on learned patterns; this can produce very capable-seeming behavior without implying human-like understanding.

questions.context: A generative AI model produces two different answers to the exact same prompt on two separate runs.
questions.question: What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Sampling randomness (e.g. temperature) in how the next word is chosen
The model has a permanent memory of the first answer that it now contradicts
The company's servers are broken
This can never happen with generative models

questions.explanation: Generative models often sample from a probability distribution over possible next words, so with non-zero randomness settings, outputs can vary between runs.

questions.context: A generative model is fine-tuned specifically on a company's internal support tickets to better match its tone and terminology.
questions.question: This process is best described as:

options.text: Fine-tuning — adapting a pre-trained model with additional task/domain-specific training
Foundation model pre-training from scratch
Manual rule scripting
Database normalization

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning takes an already pre-trained (foundation) model and further trains it on a narrower, domain-specific dataset.

questions.context: A team asks whether their LLM 'understands' legal contracts the way a lawyer does.
questions.question: What is the most defensible answer?

options.text: It recognizes patterns common in legal text but does not have verified legal reasoning or accountability like a licensed professional
Yes, it is functionally identical to a lawyer in all respects
No, it cannot process legal text in any way
It is impossible for AI to output anything related to law

questions.explanation: LLMs can produce plausible legal-sounding text from patterns in training data, but this is distinct from verified professional judgment and accountability.

questions.context: An AI vendor claims their model 'reasons' step by step to solve math problems.
questions.question: What technique most directly supports multi-step reasoning in LLM outputs?

options.text: Disabling the model's ability to generate punctuation
Removing all training data related to numbers
Chain-of-thought prompting, where the model is guided to produce intermediate reasoning steps
Reducing the vocabulary size of the model

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought approaches explicitly encourage the model to produce intermediate reasoning before a final answer, often improving accuracy on multi-step problems.

questions.context: A generative AI model outputs a block of code that looks syntactically correct but calls a function that doesn't exist in the specified library.
questions.question: What does this best illustrate?

options.text: The programming language itself is broken
This proves the model has no knowledge of any programming language
This means the company's compiler is misconfigured
The model can hallucinate plausible-looking but incorrect technical details, including nonexistent APIs

questions.explanation: Hallucination isn't limited to factual claims — models can also invent plausible-sounding but nonexistent function names, APIs, or library methods.

questions.context: A company is deciding between a small, fast model and a larger, slower model for a real-time chat feature.
questions.question: What is a key general trade-off between these options?

options.text: Model size has no effect on response quality or latency
Smaller models always outperform larger ones on every task
Larger models often produce higher-quality responses but with more latency and compute cost
Larger models are always faster and cheaper to run

questions.explanation: There is typically a trade-off between model size/capability and inference speed/cost, which teams must balance for their use case.

questions.context: An LLM-based system is described as being able to process both text and images in the same conversation.
questions.question: This capability is best described as:

options.text: A simple text macro
Multimodal AI
Single-modal AI
A relational database join

questions.explanation: Multimodal AI systems can process and/or generate more than one type of data (e.g. text and images) within the same model or pipeline.

questions.context: A generative model consistently produces longer, more verbose answers when the prompt itself is longer and more detailed.
questions.question: What does this suggest about prompt-output relationships?

options.text: The style and content of the prompt strongly influences the style and content of the generated output
Prompt length has zero effect on output
The model ignores the prompt entirely
Output length is fixed regardless of input

questions.explanation: Generative models are highly sensitive to prompt framing — including tone, length, and detail — which shapes the resulting output.

questions.context: A developer notices the same LLM performs much better on a coding task when given a clear docstring and example versus just a function name.
questions.question: What does this best demonstrate?

options.text: This has nothing to do with the prompt's content
The function name is irrelevant to any AI system
In-context learning — the model uses information provided directly in the prompt to improve its output
The model secretly retrains itself between requests

questions.explanation: In-context learning refers to a model adapting its behavior based on examples or information given directly within the prompt, without updating its weights.

questions.context: A team is comparing 'zero-shot' and 'few-shot' prompting approaches for a classification task.
questions.question: What is the key difference between them?

options.text: Zero-shot gives no examples in the prompt, while few-shot includes a handful of examples to guide the model
Zero-shot always requires model retraining, few-shot never does
They are the exact same technique with different names
Few-shot only works with image models, not text models

questions.explanation: Zero-shot prompting asks the model to perform a task with no examples; few-shot prompting provides a small number of examples within the prompt to guide behavior.

questions.context: A model is described as having been trained using human feedback to prefer helpful, harmless responses over unhelpful ones.
questions.question: This training approach is best known as:

options.text: Manual database indexing
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
Unsupervised clustering
Static rule injection

questions.explanation: RLHF is a widely used technique where human preference judgments are used to further train a model toward more helpful and safe behavior.

questions.context: An AI system generates a syntactically valid SQL query, but the query references a table name that doesn't exist in the actual database.
questions.question: What is happening here?

options.text: The database itself has a bug
This means SQL cannot be generated by AI
The query is guaranteed to still execute successfully
The model hallucinated a plausible-sounding but incorrect schema detail

questions.explanation: Without access to the actual schema, a generative model may produce plausible-looking queries referencing tables or columns that don't actually exist.

questions.context: A generative AI model's response quality noticeably degrades when the conversation history becomes very long.
questions.question: What is the most likely underlying cause?

options.text: The user's internet connection caused this
The context window is being approached or exceeded, reducing the influence of earlier content
The model's training data was deleted mid-conversation
This never actually happens with any model

questions.explanation: As conversations grow long, they can approach or exceed the model's context window, causing earlier information to have less influence on generation.

questions.context: A company wants an AI system that can browse the web and pull in current data before answering, rather than relying only on its training data.
questions.question: This need is most directly addressed by:

options.text: Reducing the model's context window to zero
Connecting the model to a retrieval or browsing tool
Making the model's vocabulary larger
Disabling all of the model's training data

questions.explanation: Retrieval or browsing tools let a model access current, external information at query time, addressing the limitation of a static training cutoff.

questions.context: A generative model is asked to translate a sentence into a language it saw very little of during training, and the translation is noticeably worse than for a well-represented language.
questions.question: What does this best illustrate?

options.text: All languages are represented identically regardless of training data
The model is incapable of translation entirely
This proves the model has a permanent hardware fault
Model performance is influenced by how much relevant data it saw during training

questions.explanation: A model's proficiency in a given task or language is strongly shaped by how much and how well-represented that data was during training.

questions.context: A researcher explains that image-generation models learn to produce images by gradually removing noise from a random starting pattern.
questions.question: This class of generative technique is most closely associated with:

options.text: A basic if-else conditional
Diffusion models
Relational database triggers
A simple lookup table of pre-made images

questions.explanation: Diffusion models generate content (often images) by learning to progressively denoise a random starting signal into a coherent output.

questions.context: A candidate writes the prompt: 'Summarize this 10-page report in 3 bullet points, focusing only on financial risks, for a non-technical executive audience.'
questions.question: What makes this a strong prompt?

options.text: It specifies format, focus area, length, and audience — all key context for a targeted output
It is short, and short prompts are always best regardless of content
It avoids giving the AI any constraints
It uses only technical jargon to sound professional

questions.explanation: Effective prompts typically specify the desired format, scope, length, and audience, since each of these shapes what a 'good' output looks like.

questions.context: A user prompt reads only: 'Make this better.' with a document attached.
questions.question: What is the core weakness of this prompt?

options.text: It is too long for the AI to process
It contains too many technical details
It cannot be understood by any AI system at all
It doesn't define what 'better' means — clarity, tone, length, structure, etc. are all left ambiguous

questions.explanation: Vague prompts leave the criteria for success undefined, so the assistant has to guess what 'better' means, often producing a mismatched result.

questions.context: A developer's prompt reads: 'Refactor this function so it runs in O(n) instead of O(n^2), and explain what changed.'
questions.question: Why is specifying the complexity goal helpful here?

options.text: This makes the prompt too long to process
AI assistants cannot understand complexity notation
It gives the AI a precise, measurable target rather than a vague notion of 'improvement'
Complexity goals are irrelevant to code quality

questions.explanation: Precise, measurable goals (like a specific time complexity target) give the AI clear criteria to optimize toward, rather than an ambiguous request.

questions.context: A prompt engineer adds 'Respond only in valid JSON matching this schema' to a data-extraction prompt.
questions.question: What is the primary benefit of this instruction?

options.text: It constrains the output format so it can be reliably parsed by downstream code
It makes the AI generate longer responses
JSON formatting has no effect on how the output can be used
It prevents the AI from understanding the task

questions.explanation: Explicit format constraints (like a JSON schema) make AI output far easier to reliably parse and integrate into other systems.

questions.context: Two prompts ask for a blog post: Prompt A says 'write about AI'; Prompt B specifies the audience, tone, length, and 3 key points to cover.
questions.question: Which prompt is more likely to need fewer revisions, and why?

options.text: Both are equally likely to need the same number of revisions regardless of detail
Prompt length has no bearing on output quality
Prompt B, because specific constraints reduce the range of plausible (but possibly unwanted) outputs
Prompt A, because vagueness always produces better creative writing

questions.explanation: More specific prompts narrow down what the model needs to produce, generally reducing back-and-forth revision compared to vague requests.

questions.context: A user asks an AI assistant to 'explain quantum computing' without specifying an audience.
questions.question: What risk does this create?

options.text: There is no risk since audience never matters
The explanation might be pitched at the wrong level — too technical or too simplified for the actual reader
The AI will refuse to answer the question
This guarantees a factually incorrect answer

questions.explanation: Without specifying the audience, the assistant has to guess the appropriate level of depth and terminology, which can easily mismatch the actual reader's needs.

questions.context: A prompt says: 'Here are 3 examples of how we write commit messages. Now write a commit message for this diff.'
questions.question: This prompting technique is best known as:

options.text: Database normalization
Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Reinforcement learning

questions.explanation: Providing a handful of examples directly in the prompt to guide the style/format of the output is the core idea of few-shot prompting.

questions.context: A candidate is asked to explain why 'act as an expert code reviewer and point out any security issues' is a more effective prompt than 'check this code.'
questions.question: What is the key difference?

options.text: The role and specific focus area (security) give the assistant a clearer lens through which to evaluate the code
The word 'expert' makes the AI factually smarter
Both prompts are functionally identical
Assigning a role has no effect on output focus

questions.explanation: Framing a role and specific evaluation criteria helps the assistant focus its analysis on the aspects that actually matter to the requester.

questions.context: A user's prompt to an AI coding assistant says: 'Write a function.' with no other detail, and the assistant asks several clarifying questions before proceeding.
questions.question: How should this behavior be interpreted?

options.text: As a failure, since the AI should always guess silently
As proof the AI cannot write any code
As irrelevant since clarifying questions are never useful
As appropriate behavior — the assistant is seeking necessary context rather than guessing

questions.explanation: When a prompt is too underspecified to proceed reliably, an assistant asking clarifying questions is a sign of good practice, not failure.

questions.context: A prompt reads: 'Do NOT include any personal opinions; only summarize the factual findings of the study.'
questions.question: What is this instruction primarily controlling?

options.text: The programming language used to generate the answer
The physical hardware running the model
The company's internal HR policy
The tone and content boundaries of the output

questions.explanation: Explicit boundary instructions like this directly shape what kind of content the model should or shouldn't include in its response.

questions.context: An engineer compares two prompts for debugging help: one includes the error message and relevant code; the other just says 'my code doesn't work.'
questions.question: Which is more likely to get a useful response, and why?

options.text: Both are equally useful since AI can diagnose any issue with zero information
The vague one, since AI performs worse with more context
Neither will ever produce a useful response
The one with the error message and code, since it gives the assistant concrete information to diagnose the issue

questions.explanation: Providing concrete diagnostic information (error messages, relevant code) gives the assistant something specific to reason about, rather than guessing blindly.

questions.context: A prompt asks the AI to 'critique this essay as if you were a strict university professor grading for logical structure.'
questions.question: This is an example of:

options.text: A request unrelated to prompt engineering
A technique that guarantees factual accuracy
Persona/role-based prompting to shape the evaluation lens and tone
A prompt that AI models cannot process

questions.explanation: Assigning a persona or role in a prompt is a common technique to steer the tone, focus, and rigor of the assistant's response.

questions.context: A user repeatedly gets overly long AI responses and adds 'Answer in 2 sentences or fewer' to future prompts.
questions.question: What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Iterating on prompt constraints based on observed output problems
That AI responses cannot be controlled in length at all
That sentence limits are ignored by all AI models
That this instruction has no effect on the output

questions.explanation: Refining prompts based on what went wrong in previous outputs (like excessive length) is a core practical prompt-engineering skill.

questions.context: A prompt provides the AI with a company style guide and says 'follow this style guide exactly when writing the response.'
questions.question: What is the main purpose of including the style guide?

options.text: To make the prompt too long to process
Style guides have no effect on generated text
To prevent the AI from producing any output
To ground the output in specific, concrete formatting/tone rules rather than the model's default style

questions.explanation: Providing explicit reference material like a style guide gives the model concrete rules to follow, rather than relying on its default stylistic tendencies.

questions.context: An AI coding assistant is asked: 'Write a function to validate emails' with no further detail, and produces code that rejects some valid but unusual email formats.
questions.question: What could have prevented this mismatch?

options.text: Nothing could have prevented this under any circumstances
Choosing a different programming language would have fixed it automatically
This is not related to prompt specificity at all
Specifying the validation rules or edge cases expected (e.g. which formats must be supported)

questions.explanation: Without explicit validation rules or edge cases, the assistant has to guess the intended scope, which can lead to mismatched behavior on ambiguous cases.

questions.context: A user's prompt says: 'Rewrite this paragraph to be more concise, but keep all the key statistics intact.'
questions.question: Why is the added constraint about statistics useful?

options.text: It makes the paragraph longer instead of shorter
It has no effect on which content is kept
Statistics are automatically removed by all AI models
It tells the assistant which content must be preserved even while shortening the text

questions.explanation: Explicitly stating what must be preserved (like key statistics) while requesting a general change (conciseness) prevents important content from being cut.

questions.context: A prompt engineer tests the same instruction phrased as a question versus phrased as a direct command, and notices different results.
questions.question: What does this suggest about prompting?

options.text: Questions and commands are always processed identically
Small changes in prompt phrasing can meaningfully affect the assistant's output
Phrasing never affects any AI's output
This means the AI is broken

questions.explanation: AI models can be sensitive to how a request is phrased, which is why testing and refining prompt wording is a real part of prompt engineering.

questions.context: A user prompt for a coding assistant reads: 'Add comments explaining WHY each step is done, not just WHAT it does.'
questions.question: What is this instruction targeting?

options.text: The variable naming convention only
The assistant's response speed
The depth and purpose of the explanatory comments generated in the code
The programming language to be used

questions.explanation: This instruction specifically shapes the *type* of commentary requested — reasoning/purpose rather than a literal restatement of the code.

questions.context: A prompt for a data-analysis task says 'assume the reader has no statistics background; avoid jargon like p-value or confidence interval.'
questions.question: What is the primary function of this constraint?

options.text: It defines the audience's background knowledge to calibrate the explanation's complexity
It requests more statistical jargon, not less
It has no bearing on how the explanation is written
It changes the underlying data being analyzed

questions.explanation: Defining the audience's existing knowledge helps the assistant choose appropriate vocabulary and depth for the explanation.

questions.context: An AI assistant given a poorly-specified prompt produces a technically correct but unhelpful answer; the user then adds more context and gets a much better result.
questions.question: What does this illustrate about the AI-assisted workflow?

options.text: The first response was random and unrelated to the prompt
Adding context never changes AI output
This means the AI understood the first prompt perfectly
Prompt quality directly and significantly affects output usefulness

questions.explanation: This is a direct illustration of how refining and adding context to a prompt can substantially improve the usefulness of the resulting output.

questions.context: A prompt for generating test cases says: 'Include at least one edge case: empty input, maximum size input, and invalid input.'
questions.question: Why is explicitly requesting these cases valuable?

options.text: Edge cases are automatically included by every AI system without being asked
This instruction makes the AI ignore all other test cases
This has no impact on test coverage
It ensures the AI's output covers scenarios that are easy to overlook if not explicitly requested

questions.explanation: Explicitly naming important edge cases in the prompt reduces the risk that the assistant's default output overlooks them.

questions.context: A prompt asks an AI assistant to 'list the pros and cons of this approach, then recommend one, with your reasoning.'
questions.question: What does structuring the prompt this way achieve?

options.text: It confuses the AI and produces no output
It has the exact same effect as a single-word prompt
It removes the need for the AI to reason at all
It breaks the request into clear sub-steps, guiding a more organized response

questions.explanation: Breaking a complex request into explicit sub-parts tends to produce more structured, complete responses than a single vague ask.

questions.context: A user asks an AI assistant for code, then follows up with 'Now explain any assumptions you made.'
questions.question: What is the benefit of this follow-up prompt?

options.text: It has no effect since the assistant made no assumptions
It causes the assistant to regenerate unrelated code
Assumptions are irrelevant to reviewing AI-generated code
It surfaces implicit decisions the assistant made, which the user can then verify or correct

questions.explanation: Asking the assistant to state its assumptions makes implicit reasoning visible, which supports better human review of the output.

questions.context: A prompt engineer avoids the instruction 'be creative' alone and instead specifies 'use an unexpected analogy from nature to explain this concept.'
questions.question: Why might the more specific instruction work better?

options.text: Specific instructions always eliminate creativity entirely
The word 'creative' guarantees a better result on its own
Both instructions are guaranteed to produce identical output
It gives a concrete direction for creativity rather than an open-ended, ambiguous goal

questions.explanation: Concrete creative constraints (like a specific type of analogy) often produce more targeted, useful creative output than an unconstrained request.

questions.context: A user includes 'if you're not sure, say so explicitly rather than guessing' in their prompt to an AI assistant.
questions.question: What behavior is this instruction trying to encourage?

options.text: Making the assistant always guess with high confidence
This instruction has no effect on the assistant's behavior
Honest expression of uncertainty instead of confidently stated guesses
Making the assistant refuse to answer anything at all

questions.explanation: This kind of instruction nudges the model toward flagging uncertainty rather than presenting a guess with unwarranted confidence.

questions.context: A support assistant retrieves the top 3 most relevant internal documents for a query, then generates an answer grounded in them.
questions.question: This architecture is best known as:

options.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
A static FAQ page
A pure rule-based expert system
A relational database trigger

questions.explanation: RAG systems combine a retrieval step (fetching relevant documents) with a generation step (producing an answer grounded in those documents).

questions.context: A system can browse the web, call a calculator tool, and query a database autonomously to complete a multi-step research task.
questions.question: This is best described as:

options.text: A static HTML webpage
A simple text macro with no tool use
A spreadsheet formula
An AI agent using tools to accomplish a goal

questions.explanation: AI agents combine reasoning with the ability to invoke external tools (web, calculators, databases) to complete multi-step tasks autonomously.

questions.context: A workflow has an AI system first draft a report, then a second AI pass reviews and critiques the draft, then a third pass revises it based on the critique.
questions.question: This is an example of:

options.text: A traditional relational database query
A static webpage with no AI involvement
A multi-agent or multi-step AI workflow
A single-shot, one-step prompt

questions.explanation: Chaining multiple AI steps (draft fi critique fi revise) is a form of multi-step/multi-agent workflow designed to improve final output quality.

questions.context: A RAG-based assistant is asked a question outside the scope of its retrieved documents, and it responds 'I don't have enough information to answer that.'
questions.question: Why is this behavior desirable?

options.text: It proves RAG systems can never answer any question
This behavior should always be avoided regardless of context
It avoids hallucinating an answer when the grounding documents don't actually cover the topic
It means the system is broken

questions.explanation: A well-designed RAG system should decline to answer confidently when its retrieved context doesn't actually support an answer, rather than hallucinating.

questions.context: An AI agent is given the goal 'book the cheapest flight under $500' and autonomously searches multiple sites, compares prices, and completes the booking.
questions.question: What distinguishes this from a simple single-turn chatbot response?

options.text: Nothing distinguishes them; they are identical
Chatbots can also autonomously book flights by default
This requires no tool use whatsoever
The agent plans and executes a sequence of actions toward a goal, rather than producing one static response

questions.explanation: Agentic behavior involves planning and taking a sequence of actions (searching, comparing, booking) toward a goal, beyond a single generated response.

questions.context: A company builds a RAG pipeline but notices the retrieval step often returns irrelevant documents, degrading answer quality.
questions.question: What does this indicate?

options.text: Retrieval has no impact on RAG output quality
The quality of a RAG system depends heavily on the retrieval step, not just the generation model
RAG systems never depend on retrieval quality
This means the generation model itself is broken

questions.explanation: RAG output quality is a function of BOTH steps — poor retrieval will produce poor grounding, regardless of how good the generation model is.

questions.context: An agentic system is designed with a maximum number of tool calls per task, to prevent it from looping indefinitely on a hard problem.
questions.question: What risk is this design choice mitigating?

options.text: The agent's vocabulary becoming too large
The agent refusing to use any tools at all
The agent getting stuck in an unproductive loop of repeated actions without making progress
The agent running out of internet bandwidth

questions.explanation: Bounding the number of steps/tool calls is a common safeguard against agents looping indefinitely without converging on a solution.

questions.context: A multi-step AI workflow for report generation includes a dedicated 'fact-checking' step before the final report is produced.
questions.question: What is the main benefit of this dedicated step?

options.text: Fact-checking steps cannot be automated in any way
It removes the need for the earlier drafting steps
It creates an explicit checkpoint to catch errors before they reach the final output
It slows down the process with no benefit

questions.explanation: Breaking a complex task into explicit steps (including verification) creates checkpoints where errors are more likely to be caught before propagating.

questions.context: An AI agent has access to a code execution tool and uses it to test a solution before presenting the final answer to the user.
questions.question: What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Tool use combined with self-verification, improving the reliability of the final output
This means the agent has no access to any tools
Code execution tools cannot be used by AI systems
The agent is guessing randomly with no verification

questions.explanation: Using a tool (like code execution) to verify intermediate work before finalizing an answer is a key advantage of agentic, tool-using systems.

questions.context: A RAG system's retrieved documents are outdated, but the generation model still produces a confident, current-sounding answer.
questions.question: What does this scenario highlight?

options.text: This proves RAG technology doesn't actually work at all
The generation model ignored the retrieved documents entirely
RAG reduces but does not eliminate the risk of incorrect or outdated answers — retrieved content quality still matters
RAG systems are always immune to outdated information

questions.explanation: Even with retrieval grounding, if the underlying documents are stale or wrong, the generated answer can still be inaccurate — RAG reduces, but doesn't eliminate, this risk.

questions.context: An agent workflow includes a 'planning' step where the AI first outlines the sub-tasks needed before executing any of them.
questions.question: What is the benefit of an explicit planning step?

options.text: It removes the need for any of the subsequent steps
Explicit planning is only useful for human workers, never for AI
It makes the overall approach more structured and lets errors in the plan be caught before execution begins
Planning steps always slow down execution with zero benefit

questions.explanation: An explicit plan-before-execute approach allows for review and correction of the overall strategy before time is spent on individual sub-tasks.

questions.context: A company builds an agent that can query a production database but only through a read-only, permission-scoped tool.
questions.question: What is the security rationale for this design?

options.text: It limits the blast radius if the agent misbehaves or is manipulated, since it can't write or delete data
Read-only access provides no security benefit at all
This design makes the agent completely incapable of answering questions
Permission scoping only matters for human users, not AI agents

questions.explanation: Scoping an agent's tool access (e.g. read-only) is a security best practice that limits potential damage from errors or misuse.

questions.context: An AI agent is asked to complete a task that requires information the retrieval system doesn't have access to, and it fabricates a plausible-sounding source.
questions.question: What does this scenario illustrate?

options.text: RAG makes hallucination completely impossible
